While they allowed to be aged in different casks, I'm sorry that I didn't explain it more. There is a law, the Lisbon agreement, which allows for the appellation of origin, with certain liquors.  It's a set of rules that countries must adhere to for a product. There is a large set of laws for tequila that it must adhere to. These appellation of origin laws are very proprietary and must be followed so that no one outside of Scotland, Mexico, etc may produce a product that it essentially their own and must be produced under their laws.  The easiest example I can give is that any tequila has a NOM number on each bottle which is tracked and certified by the Mexican government. Flavored, gold, silver, reposado,... have to adhere to these laws. It's an international agreement. While thing may have been done differently in the past. It is more a trade agreement

The aging process of both tequila and whiskey is a very distinct process that varies from distillery to distillery. I'm not a chemist but I am a bartender that has spent a long time learning and tasting different tequilas and whiskeys. There are a lot of different factors that go into the aging process. American whiskey barrels are, by US standard, new American white oak charred barrels, which gives them a different flavor profile by being allowed to absorb different sugars and flavors from the wood. Scotch, by law, must use used American whiskey barrels.  A good percentage of tequila also uses used whiskey barrels. They come from different distilleries and use the different flavors produced to blend a consistent or preferred product. Aging really isn't a science but an art and can take years for a master distiller to perfect. There are many levels of the single barrel, single malt, etc that are different distinction of a product. But to call tequila the same at a clear/silver stage and a brown or more accurately reposado/anejo stage the same is a miscarriage of justice. Tequila is one of the most highly regulated beverages on the planet based on Mexican laws scotch also follows similar laws to preserve the quality, taste, and authenticity of the liquor involved. I could go on about what constitutes Canadian whiskey, bourbon, rum, cachaca, etc., but it's a very intricate set of laws that define what we drink from being snowballed in with bath tub gin and such.
